merges.statement: Fit a recall hint to the kind of miss, naming a near spelling or another taught word rather than just saying wrong, and give the word on the second miss.

folded_records.statement: In a recall task, say what kind of near miss an answer is, the right word misspelt or another taught word that fits, rather than marking it plainly wrong.
folded_records.detail: Say it back and key words are marked in code, and a test checks that a slip is named and that the second miss gives the answer. In say it back, a near spelling of a key word of five letters or more is named with a note to check its spelling, and the sentence still counts as said; in key words, a near spelling gets "Nearly. That is the word, but the spelling is not right yet." Another word of the deck that also fits the gap is no miss: the student is told it fits the sentence too and asked for the word with the meaning given.

merges.why: Both records come from the same code in the key-word marking and state one learning: sort a recall miss by its kind (the right word misspelt, or another taught word) and answer it for that kind, not with a bare wrong. One is filed under marking and one under hints. Naming the near miss is the hint fitted to the miss, so the marking record is a special case of the hint record. The hint record is broader: it also covers any other miss and giving the word on the second miss, which both records' evidence shows. Neither record was on record before this run, so the broader one is kept and takes the merged statement. The related hint rules that were already on record (help after a try, every rung adds something, advance only on a changed answer) say different things and are left alone.

merges.statement: Check wrong-option feedback for the right answer said in other words, which a word-match check misses and a truth check never asks about.

folded_records.statement: How to catch wrong-option feedback that gives the answer away in other words, which a word-overlap check can't see and a truth check doesn't ask about.
folded_records.detail: In a ready video-essay block, one question asked how two readings interpret a contrast; its key said one reading stresses the weakness of speech and the other the power of action, and the feedback on a wrong option told the viewer that both readings put long-term power on the side of action rather than speech (`g9-transformer-runs/blocks/34c293906aa945a2.json`, lines 78 and 83). The code check for give-aways looks for runs of the answer's own words (`g9/transformer/src/mechanics/util.js`, line 116), and the judged check asks only whether each line is true to what the film had said and to the text (the same file, line 128); the line passed both, the truth check at 0.82. No check asks whether a line gives the answer away in other words.

merges.why: Both records describe the same gap in the same checks. Wrong-option feedback that restates the key in other words passes two checks: the code check, which looks only for a run of the right option's own words (both cite the same util.js line), and the judged check, which asks only whether the line is true. One record states this as the rule to check for, the other as an open question of how to catch it. The rule's own against already says a paraphrase check would need person-labelled cases before it can hold a block, so the open method question is still there after the merge. The fold adds the other record's video-essay case, scored 0.82 on truth, and its point that pointing back to what was said may count as a hint. Neither record was on record before this run. I kept the measured, held record with the larger evidence set. I left the on-record leak check by words only the key carries alone, because it states the word-based check that both of these records say misses a paraphrase.

merges.statement: After study, practise taught words by typed recall: cue each by its meaning in a one-blank sentence pointing to it alone and containing no form of it; nudge before revealing.

folded_records.statement: Teach key words by study first, then hide them and have each typed into a sentence from memory, cued by its meaning, with a nudge before the word is given.
folded_records.detail: The lesson engine's key-words block joins an animated version's keyword cards to a 3D version's recall: the student studies each word and what it means, puts the set away, and types each word into a blank in a sentence about the text, cued by its meaning (`g9/transformer/src/mechanics/key-words.js`; `g9/transformer/web/lesson.js`). Marking is code only: an exact match fills the gap, another word of the deck that also fits the sentence is not a miss, and a first miss gets a nudge, such as the word's first letter, before the second gives the word. The recall follows the study at once.

merges.why: Both new records state the same practice, drawn from the same key-words block: after study, each taught word is typed from memory into a gap sentence cued by its meaning. One adds the rules for the cue (one blank, it points to its own word, no form of the word appears). The other adds the order (study, then hide) and the nudge before the word is given. The statement keeps both. Neither was on record. I kept the record whose title names the rule and whose detail covers more of the statement. Related records already on record (two-tries-then-the-answer, retrieval-needs-a-gap, retrieval-questions-teach-not-just-measure) say different things, so I left them alone.

flags.issue: The record held two learnings. The main one stays in the statement. The second, that an advisory test still lets every such block through, is already in detail and repeats an-advisory-check-stops-nothing.
